scenes.narration: Each stage of the life of Golda Meir made the next stage possible. Golda Meir (previously Meyerson; née Mabovitch; 3 May 1898 – 8 December 1978) was the prime minister of Israel from 1969 to 1974. Born into a Ukrainian-Jewish family in Kiev, Russian Empire, Meir immigrated with her family to the United States in 1906.

The people who knew Golda Meir young describe someone already restless. In 1921, Meir and her husband immigrated to Mandatory Palestine, settling in Merhavia, later becoming the kibbutz's representative to the Histadrut. In 1934, she was elevated to the executive committee of the trade union.

What Golda Meir built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Meir held several key roles in the Jewish Agency during and after World War II. Meir was elected to the Knesset, in 1949, and served as Labor Minister until 1956, when she was appointed Foreign Minister by Prime Minister David Ben-Gurion.

By the time Golda Meir reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. In 1969, Meir assumed the role of prime minister following the death of Levi Eshkol. Early in her tenure, she made multiple diplomatic visits to western leaders to promote her vision of peace in the region.

The rise of Golda Meir was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. The outbreak of the Yom Kippur War in 1973 caught Israel off guard and inflicted severe early losses on the army. The resulting public anger damaged Meir's reputation and led to an inquiry into the failings.

Setbacks came early for Golda Meir, and the response to them is the real story. Her Alignment coalition was denied a majority in the subsequent legislative election; she resigned the following year and was succeeded as prime minister by Yitzhak Rabin. Meir died in 1978 of lymphoma and was buried on Mount Herzl.

The legacy of Golda Meir outlived the circumstances that produced it. A controversial figure in Israel, Meir has been lionized as a founder of the state and described as the "Iron Lady" of Israeli politics, but also widely blamed for the country being caught by surprise during the war of 1973. In addition, her dismissive statements towards the Palestinians have been described as the most famous example of Israeli denial of Palestinian identity.

Few lives travel as far as that of Golda Meir, and the distance is the point. Most historians believe Meir was more successful as Minister of Labour and Housing than as Premier. Meir was born Golda Mabovitch on 3 May 1898 into a Ukrainian-Jewish family in downtown Kiev in the Russian Empire.

The childhood of Golda Meir contains the adult in small print. Meir wrote in her autobiography that her earliest memories were of Moshe boarding up the front door in response to rumours of an imminent pogrom. Meir had two sisters, Sheyna (1889–1972) and Tzipora "Tzipke" (later known as Clara; born 1902–1981), as well as five other siblings who died in infancy.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Golda Meir — in that order. Moshe left Russia to find work in New York City in 1903. In his absence, the rest of the family moved to Pinsk to join Blume's family.

The turning point in the life of Golda Meir looked like a failure at the time. In 1905, Moshe moved to Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in search of higher-paying work and found employment in the workshops of the local railroad yard. The following year, he had saved up enough money to bring his family to the United States.

Every biography of Golda Meir has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Meir, along with Blume, Sheyna, and Tzipke, landed in Quebec and traveled to Milwaukee by train. By the age of eight, Meir was often put in charge of watching the store when Blume went to buy supplies.

The education of Golda Meir happened mostly outside any school. Meir attended the Fourth Street Grade School, which is now known by the Golda Meir School, from 1906 to 1912. A leader early on, she and a close friend, Regina Hamburger, organized the American Young Sisters Society, a fundraiser to pay for her classmates' textbooks in 1908.

What Golda Meir wanted at the start and what Golda Meir got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. As part of the organization's activities, Meir rented a hall and scheduled a public meeting for the event. She graduated as valedictorian of her class despite frequent tardiness due to having to work in Blume's store.

The defining trait of Golda Meir was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. In 1912, Meir began studying at North Division High School and worked part-time. The following year, Meir took a train to live with her married sister, Sheyna Korngold, in Denver, Colorado.

Those who met Golda Meir at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. The Korngolds held intellectual evenings at their home, where she was exposed to debates on Zionism, literature, women's suffrage, trade unionism, and more. In her autobiography, Meir wrote: "To the extent that my own future convictions were shaped and given form  ... those talk-filled nights in Denver played a considerable role." Around 1913, she began dating Morris Meyerson, a sign painter and socialist.

The private years of Golda Meir explain the public decades better than any speech. In 1914, after disagreements with her sister, Golda left North High School, moved out of her sister's home, and found work. After reconciling with her parents, she returned to Milwaukee and resumed studies at North Division High, graduating in 1915.

The family Golda Meir came from matters more than the legends admit. While there, she became an active member of Young Poale Zion, which later became Habonim, the Labor Zionist youth movement. She attended the teachers college Milwaukee State Normal School (now University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee) in 1916, and likely part of 1917.

The first real success of Golda Meir arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. In 1917, she took a position at a Yiddish-speaking Folks Schule in Milwaukee. On 9 July 1917, Golda became a naturalized US citizen, as her father had naturalized, and at that time children of naturalized citizens under the age of 21 received citizenship by descent.

The last chapter of Golda Meir was written long after the fame. She had intended to make aliyah (immigration to Israel) straight away, but her plans were disrupted when all transatlantic passenger services were canceled due to the entry of the United States into the First World War. A short time after their wedding, she embarked on a fund-raising campaign for Poale Zion that took her across the United States.

The whole life of Golda Meir reads like a single decision repeated. In 1921, after the conclusion of the war, the couple moved to Palestine, then part of the British Mandate, along with Meir's sister Sheyna, Sheyna's daughter, and Meir's childhood friend Regina. They sailed on the SS Pocahontas, from New York to Naples, then from there to Tel Aviv by train.

Between the birth and the legend of Golda Meir lie the years that actually decide it. They were eventually accepted into kibbutz Merhavia in the Jezreel Valley after an initial rejected application. Her duties included picking almonds, planting trees, working in the chicken coops, and running the kitchen.

The reputation of Golda Meir was built in the middle, not at the edges. Recognizing her leadership abilities, the kibbutz chose her as its representative to the Histadrut, the General Federation of Labour. In 1924, the couple left the kibbutz and lived briefly in Tel Aviv before settling in Jerusalem.

Somebody like Golda Meir should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. There, they had two children: a son Menachem in 1924, and a daughter Sarah in 1926. In 1928, Meir was elected secretary of Moetzet HaPoalot (Working Women's Council).

The life of Golda Meir begins far from where the story usually starts. She spent two years (1932–34) in the United States as an emissary for the organization and to get expert medical treatment for her daughter's kidney illness. In 1934, when Meir returned from the United States, she joined the executive committee of the Histadrut and moved up the ranks to become the head of its Political Department.

Golda Meir was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. This appointment was important training for her future role in Israeli leadership. In July 1938, Meir was the Jewish observer from Palestine at the Évian Conference, called by President Franklin D.

To understand where Golda Meir ended up, start with where Golda Meir began. Roosevelt of the United States to discuss the question of Jewish refugees' fleeing Nazi persecution. Delegates from the 32 invited countries repeatedly expressed their sorrow for the plight of the European Jews, but refused to admit the refugees.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Golda Meir ran through years nobody filmed. The only exception was the Dominican Republic, which pledged to accept 100,000 refugees on generous terms. Throughout World War II, Meir served several key roles in the Jewish Agency, which functioned as the arm of the Zionist Organization  in British Palestine.

Each stage of the life of Golda Meir made the next stage possible. In June 1946, Meir became acting head of the Political Department of the Jewish Agency after the British arrested Moshe Sharett and other leaders of the Yishuv as part of Operation Agatha. This was a critical moment in her career: she became the principal negotiator between the Jews in Palestine and the British Mandatory authorities.

The people who knew Golda Meir young describe someone already restless. After his release, Sharett went to the United States to attend talks on the UN Partition Plan, leaving Meir to head the Political Department until the establishment of the state in 1948. On 17 November 1947, shortly before the outbreak of the 1947-1949 Palestine war, Meir met with King Abdullah I of Jordan.

What Golda Meir built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. Abdullah I was seen as the only Arab leader willing to ally with a future Israeli state, as he also opposed the Mufti of Jerusalem and was rivals with other Arab countries. The meeting was cordial and confirmed that Abdullah was uninterested in invading and quietly willing to cooperate in the future.

By the time Golda Meir reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. For most of the war, Meir reluctantly played what she felt was a minor role in Israel's activities. An article published by the Golda Meir institute said "she felt she was being pushed aside to a secondary arena".

The rise of Golda Meir was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. In January 1948, the Jewish Agency needed to raise funds for the continuing war and the coming Israeli state. The treasurer of the Jewish Agency was convinced that they would not be able to raise more than $7 to $8 million from the American Jewish community.

Setbacks came early for Golda Meir, and the response to them is the real story. Key to her success was an emotional speech she first delivered in Chicago on 22 January. She toured dozens of cities in the United States and returned to Israel on 18 March.
